title: Program-as-Weights: A Programming Paradigm for Fuzzy Functions
claim: Expensive model work is done once to compile a reusable artifact, which a small local model then runs cheaply per input.
layout: 2 stacked panels, left-to-right flow, dotted arrow linking compile to run
description: Two stacked rounded black-bordered panels. The top panel, labeled 'Compile Once in the Cloud' with a cloud icon, flows left to right through three white boxes joined by gray block arrows. The first box is 'Description' with the quoted text 'Classify if this is urgent'. The second is 'Neural Compiler' with a black paw-print logo. The third is 'Neural Program', with a blue 'Discrete Text' strip and a green 'Continuous LoRA' strip. A dotted gray curved arrow runs from the Neural Program down to the bottom panel. That panel, labeled 'Run Locally' with a laptop icon, again flows left to right. It goes from 'Input' (the quoted text 'Need your signature by EOD!') to 'Neural Interpreter' (paw logo and code icon) to 'Output', shown as a red warning icon and the word 'Urgent'. The eye goes first to the bold panel titles and then follows the arrows.
caption: Overview of the Program-as-Weights paradigm. Top: compile once in the cloud. A natural-language description of a fuzzy function (here, "classify if this is urgent") is fed to a neural compiler, which produces a neural program. Bottom: run locally. A small frozen neural interpreter loads the compiled program and runs the user's input ("Need your signature by EOD!") to produce the output ("urgent"). The compiled program is a single file that can be cached, version-controlled, and called offline like any other library function.
abstract: Many everyday programming tasks resist clean rule-based implementation, such as alerting on important log lines, repairing malformed JSON, or ranking search results by intent, and are increasingly outsourced to large language model APIs at the cost of locality, reproducibility, and price. We propose fuzzy-function programming: compiling such a function from a natural-language specification into a compact, locally executable neural artifact. We instantiate this paradigm with Program-as-Weights (PAW), in which a 4B compiler trained on FuzzyBench, a 10M-example dataset we release, emits parameter-efficient adapters for a frozen, lightweight interpreter. A 0.6B Qwen3 interpreter executing PAW programs matches the performance of direct prompting of Qwen3-32B, while using roughly one fiftieth of the inference memory and running at 30 tokens/s on a MacBook M3. PAW reframes the foundation model from a per-input problem solver into a tool builder: invoked once per function definition, it produces a small reusable artifact whose subsequent calls per function application are cheap and offline.
